newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-LIFFE and Matif set accords with CME.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-LIFFE and Matif set accords with CME.

text.p: Europe's top two financial exchanges linked up with the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) on Wednesday, carving up business among them ahead of a single European currency.
The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) said it signed a deal with the CME to link short-term interest rate futures and options contracts.
At the same time, French futures and options exchange MATIF signed an accord with the CME which begins with the Matif's French bond future and will apply to all contracts of one year or more.
"This is a key element in LIFFE's EMU strategy," Jack Wigglesworth, LIFFE chairman, said in the statement.
Financial exchanges have been jostling for position ahead of the planned launch of single currency under European economic and monetary union (EMU), due to start in 1999.
Jack Sander, CME chairman, said in the LIFFE statement the link lays the groundwork for EMU.
The LIFFE link will start with three-month Euromark futures, and comes one day ahead of LIFFE's planned launch of a one-month Euromark future.

The agreement sets a trading and clearing arrangement whereby LIFFE's own short-term interest rate futures and options can be traded on CME after LIFFE has closed, extending the trading day for the LIFFE contracts.

"The Euromark is the most liquid short-term interest rate future in Europe and will settle against euros if EMU goes ahead. The link strengthens the contract and will distribute this benchmark instrument in the American time zone," Wigglesworth said.
A LIFFE official said the Euromark interest rate future would be the first contract to start trading under the new arrangement but no start data had yet been set.
"LIFFE and the CME must assess the regulatory and technical issues before reaching a formal agreement on a start date," he said. "We're at stage one, and we want to start as soon as possible."
MATIF said its agreement was initially for five years.

While the 10-year French franc bond future and options contracts will be the first to trade, the statement said the agreement applied to MATIF products with "a maturity of more than one year, denominated in francs, Ecu, the euro, or any other European currency."
